title: Zeal

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bitachon, and your line was trust. Did one worry loosen, even a little? Today, the trait that gets up and goes. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

"And Abraham rose early in the morning." That line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, opens the morning Abraham sets out for the binding of Isaac. The rabbis noticed the timing. Nothing in the command told him when to go. He could have waited a day, or a week. The text says he went at dawn. From one detail about the hour, the Talmud draws a rule that reaches every ordinary good thing a person means to do. Today's word is the trait behind that rule.
screen: `ABRAHAM ROSE EARLY.` → `NOBODY SAID WHEN.` → `ONE DETAIL, ONE RULE.`

segments.voice: Zerizut. Zeal: doing good promptly, not later. Turn it four ways. First, the rule. The Talmud, in tractate Pesachim, says the zealous are early for mitzvot, and it learns this from Abraham rising early. In Hebrew: zerizin makdimin l'mitzvot. Second, how later works. Later is a soft word. A thank-you note waits a day, then a week, and then it feels too late to send. A visit to someone who is sick waits until they're better. Zerizut is the trait that notices good things can spoil by waiting. Third, the deer. Pirkei Avot keeps a saying of Judah ben Tema: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer and strong as a lion, to do the will of your Father in heaven. Swift as a deer is zerizut. Not frantic. Swift the way a deer is swift: light, sure, already moving. Fourth, the measure. Mussar sets every trait at its right amount, and zeal has one too. Zerizut is not rushing through a prayer, or hurrying a friend who needs time, or answering before you've listened. It's closing the gap between deciding to do a good thing and doing it. And it sits beside yesterday's trust like a partner. Trust lets go of the outcome. Zeal doesn't let go of the doing. One empties the hands of worry, and the other fills them with the next good thing.
screen: `THE ZEALOUS ARE EARLY.` · `GOOD THINGS SPOIL BY WAITING.` · `SWIFT AS A DEER.` · `CLOSE THE GAP, DON'T RUSH.` · then, large: `AND ABRAHAM ROSE EARLY IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing now. Settle, and breathe. Ask what good thing you've been meaning to do. A message to someone who's struggling. A thank-you. A small repair. A donation you keep postponing. Choose one that fits inside the next two minutes. If it can be done right here, a short text, a note, a click, do it now, while the bell holds the time. If it can't, take the first step: open the message, write the name, set out the thing you'll need. If you pray, you can begin the way some Jews begin a mitzvah, by saying a blessing first. Then go. The bell holds the time.
Zerizut. Zeal: closing the gap between meaning to do good and doing it. The zealous are early for mitzvot. Today's word.

Your line: promptly. Today, the next time you catch yourself saying I'll do it later about something good, do the first piece of it before the sentence is over. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish law applies the principle that the zealous are early for mitzvot, for example by holding a baby boy's circumcision early in the day, and Mussar students practice zerizut by acting on a good intention as soon as it arises.
